1. Introduction 
The purpose of this report is to describe the data acquired for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment to facilitate 
its analysis.  The data is all digital, where the fuel was gaseous and there was no collection of soot or the 
combustion gases.  For each test, the key data consists of image files and a file with the non-imaging 
measurements.  Additional files such as chamber calculator output, camera metadata, and operational 
logs provide information that can support the analysis. 
 
It is recommended that readers interested in analyzing the CLD Flame data begin by familiarizing 
themselves with the hardware and instrumentation, either through the overview in the CLD Flame Final 
Report or the more comprehensive description found in the ACME Engineering Implementation 
document. 
 
Those seeking to analyze the data should next review this document.  To interpret the non-imaging data, 
it is suggested that a sample data file be opened, named for example 21050R1_data.csv, which has 
comma-separated values and can be opened with spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel.  The data 
is in raw voltages, where conversion to engineering units requires study of ACME’s Software Interface 
Design Description, i.e., ACME-DOC-010 (where the latest version at the time of this writing is revision D). 
Additional documents that may be important include:

Also note that the Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP) was not used during CLD Flame 
testing, and as such interpretation of its data is not addressed herein. 
 
 
2. CLD Flame Overview 
This text is the “Overview” from the ACME/CLD Flame Final Report, which also provides descriptions of the 
science, preliminary results, and more.  It is strongly suggested that it be reviewed by those interested in 
analyzing the CLD Flame data. 
 
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is one of six independent experiments that 
make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are 
conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) and Co-Investigator are respectively Profs. Marshall B. Long 
and Mitchell D. Smooke, who are both in the Department of Mechanical Engineering & Materials Science 
at Yale University.  The ISS research benefitted greatly from the work of Dr. Jesse Tinajero, who was a Yale 
postdoctoral researcher during the spaceflight operations, and Dr. Davide Giassi, who as a Yale doctoral 
student did important preparatory work.  
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including CLD Flame and the rest of the ACME investigations.  In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki 
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist.  For 
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam 
who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations for CLD Flame were conducted in three separate rounds of testing, where the rounds 
were respectively conducted during Increments 53-54, 55-56, and 64. The third round was limited in scope 
and was carried out with a replacement 20-slpm mass flow controller for the oxidizer coflow to make up 
for the poor coflow performance in the first two rounds. 
 
Note that there was a direct precursor to the CLD Flame investigation, namely the Structure & Liftoff In 
Combustion Experiment (SLICE), which was conducted in the ISS’ Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) 
during Expedition 30 in early 2012.  Prof. Long was the Principal Investigator, while Smooke, Takahashi, 
and Stocker were Co-Investigators.  For more information about SLICE, readers are encouraged to consult 
its final report.

3. Tests Conducted 
This text is an excerpt from the “Results” section of the ACME/CLD Flame – 30-Day Operation 
Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 64 (which is included in the ACME/Flame Design Final Report). 
 
Neglecting hardware set-up and engineering preparation, the first round took place from Nov. 2017 to 
Feb. 2018, during Increments 53-54, when 130 methane flames were ignited.  ACME testing subsequently 
shifted to the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment, and 
afterward returned for a second round of CLD Flame tests, which took place from May to September 2018, 
during Increments 55-56, when 162 ethylene flames were ignited.  The ‘interruption’ in the CLD Flame 
testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in 
detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
Poor performance in ramping the oxidizer coflow during early testing inhibited determination of 
extinction limits.  The decision was made to launch a replacement Mass Flow Controller (MFC) and 
conduct a limited third round of tests to address that shortcoming.  The third round with the replacement 
MFC was conducted in Feb.-March 2021, during Increment 64, when 52 ethylene and methane flames 
were ignited.  As a result, a total of 344 flames were ignited during the three rounds and five increments. 
 
CLD Flame does not have subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently 
conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both are simple hydrocarbon gases 
for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and 
tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene 
(C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with 
pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel and 
nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched with methane 
concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  Similarly, 
bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balance of 
nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and 
nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel 
concentrations.  In all cases, the coflow was 21% oxygen with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  
 
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for CLD Flame, where all of the ISS results are electronically 
transmitted to the ground.  That is furthermore the case for all currently planned ACME experiments. 
 
A summary log of the flames ignited for the CLD Flame experiment during the three rounds (Increments 
53-56 and 64), including a limited overview of the test conditions, is found in Table 1.

4. Data Interpretation 
This key section provides (1) a general description of the raw experimental data and associated files and 
(2) guidance on data conversions, e.g., to engineering units.  Only limited guidance is provided for the 
processing of image data, with the important exception of the conversion of the ACME DataCam images 
from the raw Halcon object (HOBJ) format. 
 
A. Non-Imaging Data 
Data and files discussed in this section include the following: 
Data Output File 
Mass Flow Controller (MFC) Setpoint File 
Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
 
1. Data Output File 
The basic ACME non-imaging measurements for each test are together in a file described in 
Section 8.1 Data Output File on page 124 of Software Interface Design Description (ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D).  The test number is made up of the year (2-digts), day of year (3 digits), and 
test (a letter and single-digit number).  As such, the example, 21062D2 is test D2 conducted 
on the 62nd day of 2021.  But the test could also be early on the next (e.g., 63rd) day because 
the day portion of ACME test numbers is not changed when operations continue past 
midnight (whether GMT or Eastern) into the start of the next day. 
 
Tests numbers that only differ by the final digit (e.g., 21050D1, 21050D2, and 21050D3) are 
typically similar and occasionally identical, where the number is indicative of the variant or

in ACME testing, the letter E ceased to be used because Excel software (for example) by 
default interpreted it as representing an exponential which was inconvenient.  As a related 
aside, ACME tests are often not conducted in order and some planned tests are regularly not 
conducted at all.  The latter results in additional letter gaps if the tests from a day are sorted 
alphabetically.  However, ACME testing often begins with test A1, where the final digit begins 
with 1 and is increased from there with variant or repeat tests for the same letter.

spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel.  The first row is a header and provides a limited

Metadata Header of ACME-DOC-010 Rev D, which begins on page 126.

The ACME MFCs are Hastings HFC-D-302 with default standard temperature and pressures 
(STP) of 0 Celsius and 760 torr for computations of volumetric flow or velocity.  It is very 
important to understand that slpm, i.e., standard liters per minute, is a measurement of the 
mass (or alternatively molar) flow rate which is independent of the actual temperature or 
pressure.  This is discussed for example in the MFC manual, where chapter 9 (on page 39) is 
“Volumetric vs. Mass Flow.”  Hastings’s online converter at https://massflowconverter.com/ 
may be helpful as a check in this regard. 
 
Conversions for the actual gases can be made with information provided in the manual on 
subsequent pages and the spreadsheets GasDataTables.xls and Inside gas mix calculator.xls 
which were both provided by the MFC manufacturer.  First, open GasDataTables.xls and 
enable content, and then open Inside gas mix calculator.xls and enable content.  From this, 
one should be able to enter mixtures and compute appropriate Gas Conversion Factors 
(GCFs).

2. Mass Flow Controller (MFC) Setpoint File 
While the basic data file includes measurement of the gas flow rates, it may be helpful to 
understand the intended flow rates, where that information is found in a separate file for 
each test with a name like 21050R1_mfcSetpoints.csv.  While it shares strong similarities to 
the basic data file, the rows of data are not added at a continuous and consistent rate.  The 
file is briefly discussed in section 8.2 Mass Flow Controller Setpoint File on page 124 of ACME-
DOC-010 Rev D.   
 
3. Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) data 
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) in which the experiment was conducted, was equipped 
with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS), but it was not utilized for ACME testing because 
of the need for crew time to enable and disable the isolation (by respectively removing and 
installing alignment guides) on each test day.  However, the CIR was equipped with a 3-axis 
SAMS sensor head.  The acceleration archives, along with relevant documentation, are 
accessible from https://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/pims/home/, the home page for the Principal 
Investigator Microgravity Services (PIMS). 
 
The following guidance for the SAMS data was provided by Kenneth Hrovat (NASA Glenn):  In 
addition to the documentation and links from the PIMS home page, we introduce a few ways 
below to get started with exploring the CIR microgravity environment taking the perspective 
of SAMS measurements from within the rack. 
 
Roadmap Spectrograms 
To get a high-level, spectral roadmap view within two days after measurement, you can: 
a. Use your browser and start at this link: http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/roadmap 
b. In the upper left pane, you can navigate by GMT date to see a list of plots (PDF files) 
in the right pane for the GMT date of your choice.  We refer to these PDFs as roadmap 
plots.  For SAMS, these are acceleration spectrograms, which for vibratory data are a 
good way to look at patterns, structures and boundaries in both time and frequency 
for long time spans -- nominally, 8 hours per plot.  These spectrograms are mostly 
qualitative and crudely quantitative three-dimensional plots in that a color scale 
attempts to map power spectral density magnitude as a color for the 3rd dimension. 
NOTE: Ticking the Navigation Filter for “es05” in the bottom pane will then only 
highlight days in yellow in the upper left pane when the operations team powered on 
the SAMS sensor in the CIR to take measurements. 
c. You might want to navigate directly to a GMT day of interest for your science 
operations or run, but you can also browse day-by-day too in order to get some 
context comparing various 8-hour spans to get a feel for the environment under 
various conditions.

B. Image Files 
Image data and files discussed in this section are associated with the following cameras: 
Analog, operations (ops), internal camera 
ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) intensified camera 
 
High Bit-depth Multi-spectral (HiBMs) camera and CIR illumination package 
 
The Low Light Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) camera is not addressed herein because it was not used 
for CLD Flame.  Of the ACME investigations, the LLL-UV camera was only used by the Structure 
and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) study. 
 
1. Analog, internal, operations (ops) camera  
This color analog camera is mounted on the ACME chamber insert, and as such is within the 
combustion chamber during testing and is sometimes referred to as the internal camera.  Its 
primary purpose is to support the operations, e.g., to visualize the burner and igniter, and as 
such is also often referred to as the operations or ops camera. 
 
The NTSC video (named for the National Television System Committee) from the ops camera 
is at 29.97 frames per second (fps) or nominally 30 fps.  It is not recorded on the space station 
but is streamed to the ground in near real time and is recorded on CIR consoles at the Glenn 
ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC) in a Transport Stream (TS) format using VLC Media 
Player, which can be freely downloaded from https://www.videolan.org/vlc/.  That software 
has a snapshot function allowing for convenient extraction of still images, e.g., for making 
measurements of flame dimensions. 
 
2. ACME Data Camera (DataCam) 
ACME’s primary camera is a high-definition (1360 x 1024), 12-bit color camera mounted 
outside the chamber on CIR’s optical bench.  It is equipped with a motorized lens with 
independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  It has a filter barrel with a fused silica 
window (for color imaging), a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, and bandpass filters for 
imaging CH* and CH2O (formaldehyde) chemiluminescence. 
 
It was characterized prior to launch to enable temperature measurements via soot pyrometry 
and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP), soot volume fraction, and quantitative determination of 
the CH* concentration.

Images were normally downlinked within a week of the testing, but selected images were 
often downlinked during a test day.  Regardless, the images were downloaded in a wrapped 
Halcon object (HOBJ) format, which is not readily opened with typical image processing 
software.  The image data was made available in that raw format and later in a converted TIFF 
format, where the NASA conversion was carried out without each of the following: 
• 
color balancing (to avoid possible saturation as subsequently discussed)  
• 
dark frame subtraction 
• 
removal of hot spots from dead pixels (e.g., resulting from radiation damage)  
Furthermore, the NASA conversion employed a standard bilinear demosaicing process which 
is detrimental when determining temperature profiles via Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) as it 
will average pixels both on and off the glowing fibers.  The priority in the NASA conversion 
was to make the images more readily accessible, not to meet all needs. 
 
Most ACME investigators are processing the raw HOBJ files using the OMA2 software 
developed by Prof. Marshall Long (Yale U.), the lead for ACME’s CLD Flame experiment.   The 
OMA2 software is freely available in both Mac and cross-platform (Qt) versions, where the 
latter can be used with both PC and Linux operating systems.  A tutorial was prepared by Dr. 
Jesse Tinajero on the use of OMA2 to process ACME’s HOBJ image files, where it can be found 
at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RMtu3KEXNiI.  It has also been broken up and posted 
in three parts in which the image resolution may be better: 
 
Part 1 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdQHeQwokvY 
 
Part 2 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mua_8CfqhfM

The OMA2 read-hobj function was also rewritten by Tinajero as a Python function, where 
Python is an open source programming language that is easily obtainable for MacOS, Linux, 
and Windows operating systems.  The Python script to open the HOBJ files can be downloaded

1. CIR chamber calculator file 
In great contrast to other file types, there is just a single chamber calculator file for the second 
and third of CLD Flame’s three rounds of testing:  
 
Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2018-05-22 to 2018-09-19.xlsx 
 
Final ACME Chamber Calculator - 2021-02-03 to 2021-03-09.xlsx 
These files provide estimates of the composition of the combustion chamber before and after 
each test, and more generally for every Fuel/Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) action 
involving gas flow into or out of the chamber.  This includes filling and venting operations, 
plus any recirculation of the chamber contents through the adsorber cartridge filled with 13x 
molecular sieves. 
 
Meanwhile, this data was not recorded during the first round of CLD Flame testing.  During 
CLD Flame testing, however, the combustion chamber was almost always filled with nitrogen 
– and no oxygen!  The oxygen wasn’t needed because of the presence of the coflow of 
synthetic air, i.e., a 21/79 mixture of oxygen/nitrogen on a volume (molar) basis.  
Furthermore, the small flames and limited test durations in the CLD Flame testing had a 
limited effect on the chamber pressure and composition. 
 
The chamber calculator provides the chamber pressure before and after each operation 
involving flow into or out of the chamber.  While the standard ACME data output files 
(discussed in section 4.A.1) provide the chamber pressure throughout each test, that 
measurement is from a pressure transducer that hadn’t been calibrated for years.  
Meanwhile, the calibrations of the corresponding CIR pressure transducers are checked every 
six months and those calibrations are updated if needed.  Therefore, the chamber calculator 
is the more reliable source of the chamber pressure. 
 
The pressure in the CIR chamber is measured by four different CIR pressure transducers, of 
which one (PT29) is a different model used for safety.  The output of the other three

In a test, the chamber calculator assumes either complete combustion or no combustion, 
where in the former case the reactant flowing from the burner is transformed into carbon 
dioxide and water vapor (or water vapor alone if the fuel was hydrogen).  Failed or 
unsustained ignitions were typically set to assume no ignition.  Short-lived flames were often 
treated as having complete combustion, even if a significant fraction of the reactant didn’t 
burn.  Adjustments can be made, however, to account for partial combustion by appropriate 
selection of the ‘Burn Fraction’ in column AL. 
 
With recirculation of the chamber contents, the calculator assumes that the carbon dioxide 
and water vapor are completely adsorbed, i.e., removed from the chamber.  Meanwhile, it 
assumes that any unburnt fuels are not adsorbed.  For CLD Flame testing, however, the 
recirculation typically only occurred at the end of CLD Flame test days because of the presence 
of the coflow. 
 
Researchers can of course make their estimates of the chamber contents, but the chamber 
calculator should nonetheless be referenced for its record of fills, venting, and recirculation.  
Note that the chamber’s free volume is approximately 83 liters depending on the installed 
hardware.

Nomenclature 
This document’s key abbreviations are listed here.

Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (project including s- Flame)

Area of Interest (e.g., for image acquisition of just a portion of the camera FOV) 
ASCII 
American Standard Code for Information Interchange 
BRE 
Burning Rate Emulator (an ACME experiment) 
CCD 
Charge-Coupled Device (such as a camera sensor) 
CIR 
Combustion Integrated Rack (ISS facility in which ACME experiments are conducted) 
CFI 
Cool Flames Investigation (a droplet combustion experiment preceding ACME in the CIR) 
CFI-G 
Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (an ACME experiment selected by CASIS and NSF) 
CLD Flame 
Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (another ACME experiment) 
CSV 
comma-separated values 
DataCam 
Data Camera (for ACME experiments, characterized for pyrometry, etc.) 
E-FIELD Flames Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames 
Fiji 
Fiji Is Just ImageJ (a version of ImageJ preloaded with many plug-in features) 
Flame Design 
another ACME experiment 
FOMA 
Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (CIR’s gas management subsystem) 
FOV 
Field of View 
fps 
frames per second 
GCIP 
Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package 
GIPOC 
Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center 
GMT 
Greenwich Mean Time 
HiBMs 
High Bit-depth Multi-spectral camera (of the CIR facility) 
HOBJ 
Halcon object (binary uncompressed format; used for the DataCam)

Image Processing and Analysis in Java (open-source image processing software)  
IPSU 
Image Processing and Storage Unit (CIR subsystem)

IPSU for Gigabit ethernet cameras 
ISS 
International Space Station 
LLL-UV 
Low Light Level Ultraviolet camera (of the CIR facility) 
MFC 
Mass Flow Controller 
NTSC 
National Television System Committee 
OMA2 
Optical Multi-channel Analyzer 2 (open-source software for image processing and display) 
ops 
operations

Passive Rack Isolation System

Principal Investigator Microgravity Services 
PMT 
Photomultiplier Tube (where ACME is equipped with three PMT modules)

pressure transducer

pounds per square inch

slpm
